output_guides.short: Add concrete detail, structured bullets, comparisons, and examples without filler. If evidence is limited, state assumptions briefly and still complete every required section. Keep the answer detailed but bounded so it can finish within the allotted token budget. Prioritize the most decision-useful facts first and stop once every requested section is complete.
output_guides.long: Expand each section with evidence, comparisons, reasoning, and actionable detail without repetition. Balance coverage across sections so the report remains consistently useful. Keep the report detailed but bounded so it can finish within the allotted token budget. Prioritize the most important companies, scenarios, assumptions, and recommendations first, then stop once all requested sections are complete.
output_guides.planning: Keep the planning memo detailed but bounded. Focus on the most useful workstream structure, metrics, source guidance, validation steps, and integration checks. Stop once every requested section is complete.
output_guides.synthesis: Ensure no data is lost and resolve contradictions between sources. Keep the final report detailed but bounded so it can finish within the allotted token budget. Prioritize the sections that matter most for executive decision making, then stop once all required sections are complete.

agents.goal: Decompose the analysis request into a structured research framework with four workstreams
agents.backstory: Senior strategist who excels at breaking complex problems into parallel sub-tasks.

agents.goal: Quickly gather key market statistics and figures
agents.backstory: Efficient data analyst who rapidly extracts essential numbers from market reports.

agents.goal: Produce an exhaustive, deeply-reasoned analysis covering technology and competitive dynamics
agents.backstory: World-class industry analyst known for thorough, multi-dimensional reports. You always provide detailed SWOT analysis, technology evaluations, and quantitative comparisons. Your reports are comprehensive and data-rich.

agents.goal: Identify emerging trends and regional patterns concisely
agents.backstory: Trend-spotting specialist who delivers punchy summaries of emerging patterns across regions.

agents.goal: Quickly evaluate key risks and regulatory challenges
agents.backstory: Risk analyst who delivers concise risk assessments covering regulatory, technical, and geopolitical factors.

agents.goal: Merge all research streams into a single cohesive executive report
agents.backstory: Expert report writer who unifies diverse inputs into polished, publication-ready documents.

tasks.description:
MANDATORY SCOPE: You are the Planning Coordinator. Research domain is the topic "{topic}" and the analysis year is {year}. Treat the topic as a full industry or market program, not a one-line keyword. Your output will gate four downstream parallel workstreams. Any omission at planning time will force rework later, so be exhaustive in structure even if the topic is narrow.

OBJECTIVE: Produce a single integrated research framework and planning memo. The framework must be operational: another analyst could follow it without asking follow-up questions. Use numbered sections and sub-bullets. Do not default to generic consulting boilerplate: anchor every workstream to specifics implied by the topic and year.

WORKSTREAM A (Market and Quantitative Dossier): Define total addressable market thinking, key quantitative indicators, segment cut logic, pricing or unit economics if relevant, and the minimum charts or tables the Data Collector should aim to support. List at least six explicit questions. Specify preferred source classes (e.g. regulatory filings, trade press, industry associations, company earnings, third-party market studies) and how to triangulate when sources conflict. Add a sub-section on data quality, revision risk, and how to express confidence bands. Include a one-paragraph example of a "complete" numeric snapshot for a comparable industry to illustrate density expectations.

WORKSTREAM B (Strategic, Technology, and Competition): Map which technology vectors matter for {topic} in {year}, which competitive layers exist, and which firms or archetypes to benchmark. List at least eight questions, including M&A, partnerships, and talent. Define how the Deep Analyst should sequence depth versus breadth, and which SWOT or scenario templates to use. Add explicit instruction on disambiguating incumbents vs insurgents, direct vs platform competitors, and ecosystem complements.

WORKSTREAM C (Geography, Regulation, and Macro Context): State how to split regions, what local regulatory or trade angles matter, and which macro drivers may dominate (rates, energy, policy shocks). List at least six questions. Direct the Trend Scout to watch both established regions and at least one emerging market cluster, with a note on what "surprise" signals to track. Add guidance on time horizon for trends (12, 24, 36 months) and how to connect regional stories without double-counting global totals.

WORKSTREAM D (Risk, Resilience, and Gating Decisions): Define the risk rubric, including how to keep regulatory, technology, and geopolitical risks in one comparable matrix, how to define triggers and leading indicators, and how the Risk Assessor should separate headline noise from material exposure for participants in {topic}. List at least seven questions. Add a subsection on second-order and cascade effects, plus how risks tie back to financial or operational levers. Include a short narrative on what "escalation" to the synthesis phase should look like if two workstreams conflict.

CROSS-CUTTING REQUIREMENTS: (1) A dependency graph in prose: which workstream feeds which synthesis subsection. (2) A unified glossary of terms that might be used inconsistently (define acronyms on first use in the plan). (3) An integration checklist: before synthesis, the Report Synthesizer must verify that each figure, claim, and recommendation can be traced to at least one of the workstreams. (4) A "non-goals" list: what the research will explicitly not cover to prevent scope explosion. (5) A schedule suggestion: if parallel work completes out of order, how to hold partial results without blocking others.

FORMATTING: Use clear section headers, dense but readable bullets, and a final "Planning Memo Summary" that is no more than 15 bullets but could stand alone. Write as a substantial planning memo, not a short note.

STAKEHOLDERS AND CONSUMERS: Name implied reader personas (e.g. product leadership, GTM, finance, public policy) and one bullet each on what they must extract from workstreams A-D. Add a short RACI-style note: who is "accountable" for numbers vs narrative vs risk calibration in the final synthesis, even as a research-only exercise without real names.

SUCCESS CRITERIA AND KPIs: Define 8-10 measurable "research quality" KPIs the program should satisfy (e.g. every segment claim tied to a source class, every risk with a named trigger, every region with a quant or explicit gap). Add a red-team subsection: which biases (survivorship, recency, vendor hype) the teams must name up front and how to counter them.

SCENARIO SHELL FOR DOWNSTREAM: Provide a compact empty template listing scenario axes that Deep Analyst and Trend Scout may reuse (e.g. regulation tight vs light, interest-rate stress, technology adoption fast vs slow, fragmentation vs consolidation) so that parallel teams do not invent incompatible dimensions.

ASSUMPTION VERSIONING: Require an "Assumptions register" in the plan: list global assumptions (FX, inflation, definition of the market boundary, whether services are in-scope) and how a change in each would swing conclusions. Tag each with sensitivity (low vs high).

DELIVERABLE SPECS: For each workstream, specify the minimum acceptable length or density for the first draft (e.g. number of data points, number of named firms, number of risk rows) as guidance, not as rigid word counts, so downstream agents calibrate effort.

CITATION CONVENTIONS: Instruct a consistent in-text style for the parallel drafts (e.g. bracket source tags, short codes for analyst reports) to reduce merge pain at synthesis. Note how to mark model-inferred content versus sourced content.

DEFINITION-OF-DONE: Spell out a merge-ready definition: every numeric claim in any draft must be tagged as sourced, model-estimated, or missing; every region block must have either a hard number or an explicit null; every risk row must be assigned a notional product or finance owner even in draft form.

PRE-MORTEM: Add a short subsection: if the final synthesis fails board review, list the top three structural failure modes in the parallel plan (e.g. double-counted TAM, misaligned risk severity, or inconsistent tech taxonomy) and how you prevented them in the workstream spec.

TRADE, EXPORT, AND SENSITIVITY: If the topic is technology, defense-adjacent, or dual-use, add a line in the plan on how the teams should treat export-control, sanctions, and dual-use language without over-claiming legal conclusions; instruct them to mark speculation.

DATA ETHICS AND PII: Add one paragraph on not inventing private company internals, PII, or wiretap-grade competitive intelligence, and to prefer public or licensed sources even when a vivid story would be convenient.

CONFLICT RESOLUTION: Define an ordering rule for numeric conflicts: prefer primary > regulatory filing > two independent analyst firms with narrow spread > model inference, and when two streams disagree on narrative, require named hypotheses and a tie-breaker test.
{output_guide}
tasks.expected_output: An even longer planning memo: all prior workstream and cross-cutting content, plus definition-of-done, pre-mortem, trade or dual-use handling, PII and ethics, conflict resolution hierarchy, and merge-ready quality gates, still tailored to the stated topic and year, ending with a 15-bullet summary.

tasks.description:
ROLE: You are the Data Collector. The planning input defines scope; your job is a dense, defensible market data brief for "{topic}" in {year}. Executives and quants will read this without the planning memo, so re-state the topic and year in one line, then go deep.

NUMERIC CORE: Report overall market size in USD (or the dominant industry convention), base year, forecast year, and CAGR with explicit time window. If multiple analyst firms disagree, show a small comparison table: source name, TAM, CAGR, and your reconciled or preferred range with rationale. If only directional data exists, state bands and the strongest weak signals.

SEGMENTATION: Top five segments by revenue (or the correct unit for the industry). For each segment: size, growth, margin proxy if knowable, one-line structural driver, and one contrarian or bear case. Call out which segments are structurally consolidating vs fragmenting.

COMPETITIVE SHARE: Name top five companies by market share (or an honest proxy: revenue share, install base, or category leadership). For each, one sentence on positioning and one on recent momentum. If share data is not public, use revenue rank with caveats and suggest how synthesis should phrase uncertainty.

DEMAND AND PRICING: Revenue drivers, pricing or subscription dynamics, customer budget cycles, and demand indicators (shipments, utilization, RFP volume, or sector-specific KPIs). Separate cyclical from secular where possible.

GEOGRAPHY: Regional revenue or growth split (Americas, EMEA, APAC at minimum, plus emerging if material). For each region, one growth outlier and one drag. Note FX or local policy sensitivity if it moves numbers.

UNCERTAINTY: Important data gaps, stale series, and confidence notes. List which numbers are model-sensitive. Add a short "if we only had one more dataset" wish list.

SOURCES: Annotated source list. Each source: name, what it supports, and limitation. Prefer primary and peer-reviewed where realistic; mark analyst estimates as such.

APPEND-STYLE DENSITY: After the main bullets, add a subsection "Additional quantitative hooks" with at least ten extra mini-facts, ratios, or year-over-year deltas that may support narrative elsewhere, even if tangential, each with a one-line caveat if needed. Do not pad with empty phrases.

UNITS AND BOUNDARY: Add an explicit call-out for whether figures are manufacturer revenue, end-customer spend, or license-only; for subscription businesses, state ARR vs GAAP if relevant. Reconcile or flag when the planning scope assumed a different boundary.

MARGIN AND CASH-ADJACENT: Where possible, add gross margin or contribution hints by segment, capex intensity, or working capital profile at industry level; if unknowable, state proxies (e.g. opex as share of revenue) and uncertainty.

COHORT AND CHANNEL: If the industry has meaningful channel (direct vs partner vs marketplace), split revenue or growth hints. If B2B vs B2C mix matters, estimate split with caveats. Add a short "adoption S-curve" position for {year} if applicable.

ALTERNATIVE SCENARIOS: Provide a one-page-equivalent in bullets: base vs downside vs upside for TAM or growth, with the single biggest driver of each case and a probability-style verbal label (e.g. "plausible / tail").

PEER BENCHMARK: Add a subsection comparing this market to two adjacent or analogous markets on growth, margin, and capital intensity, with explicit caveats on comparability.

HISTORICAL BASELINE: Where possible, include at least three historical anchor points (e.g. TAM in year-2, year-1, and current) or explain why a series cannot be built.

REVISION LOG: If you changed your mind on a number while writing, show before/after in one line with reason (e.g. wider definition) so synthesis does not double-count.

SEASONALITY AND CYCLES: If the market has fiscal-year bias, back-to-school, holiday, project windows, or commodity cycles, state how that warps y/y comparisons and the best quarter to benchmark for {year}.

RETENTION AND EXPANSION PROXIES: For subscription or contract-heavy models, add verbal hints for gross retention, net revenue retention, or renewal rates at industry or segment level if public analogs exist; if not, list what ratio would be the best proxy to watch.

INVESTMENT INTENSITY: Add R&D as percent of sales and sales and marketing as percent of sales at industry level or for named public comparables, with caveats, plus capital intensity (capex to revenue) if the topic is asset-heavy.

EMPLOYEES AND PRODUCTIVITY: Where possible, one bullet on headcount growth vs revenue growth (rule-of-thumb productivity) and whether the industry is hiring or rationalizing in {year}.

TAX AND JURISDICTION: If profit shifting, digital services tax, or local incentives matter, add one non-legal, directional paragraph on how reported margins could differ from economic margins by region.

PUBLIC-FILING CHECKLIST: Add a 6-8 line checklist of what you would pull from 10-K/20-F/annual reports (segments, risk factors, geographic revenue) if a human analyst had more time, without fabricating that you pulled them.

BENCHMARK BASKET: Name 4-6 public tickers that best proxy this market, with one line each on why the match is imperfect, so synthesis can sanity-check TAM and multiples.

DATA LINEAGE: For your top 5 headline numbers, add a one-line "how we would verify this in a second pass" (e.g. triangulate two filings, cross-check a trade association).
{output_guide}
tasks.expected_output: An extended maximal data dossier: all prior sections plus seasonality, retention proxies, opex and capex intensity, headcount or productivity, tax and margin jurisdiction notes, 10-K checklist, public benchmark tickers, data lineage and verification steps, 10+ extra hooks, revision log, and annotated sources, for the given topic and year.

tasks.description:
CHARTER: You are the Deep Analyst. This is the highest-depth workstream for "{topic}" in {year}. The research plan is binding on scope, but you must still produce analytical surplus: scenarios, firm-level texture, and explicit trade-offs that downstream synthesis can cut if needed, but cannot invent later.

SECTION 1 - TECHNOLOGY LANDSCAPE (MAXIMUM DEPTH): Evaluate major technology vectors relevant to the industry: generative AI, classical ML, edge and on-device, multimodal, agents and automation, AI safety and alignment, energy and inference efficiency, foundation models, open vs proprietary stacks, data governance and MLOps, and domain-specific toolchains. For each selected trend, cover: current state, maturity (TRL-style if it helps), adoption curve by segment, key vendors or research fronts, and projected 24- to 60-month impact on economics and defensibility. Add a subsection on convergence (when two trends stack) and a subsection on dislocated bets (trends that look hot but have weak value capture in this market). Cite or clearly label when knowledge is model inference versus typical industry pattern.

SECTION 2 - COMPETITIVE DYNAMICS: Build a full landscape: tier-1 incumbents, fast followers, well-funded scale-ups, open-source or community alternatives, and vertical specialists. For the top three players by your judgment, do full SWOT. Add M&A and partnership review: last 24-36 months, strategic logic, and failed or stalled deals. Cover barriers to entry, switching costs, data advantages, network effects, distribution moats, and talent concentration. Add a short "wargame" paragraph: if the market leader stumbles, who benefits first and how.

SECTION 3 - STRATEGY AND RECOMMENDATIONS: Ranked investment and initiative themes by ROI and feasibility. A build vs buy vs partner decision framework with when to overrule each. Workforce and talent: roles that appreciate vs commoditize. Roadmap: 0-6 months, 6-12, 12-36 months with named milestone types, not only dates. Each recommendation: owner function, success metric, and failure mode. Add at least one "no-go" or divest scenario with triggers.

EVIDENCE DISCIPLINE: Add explicit evidence, trade-offs, and source-style attributions. If the planning memo listed questions, map which subsection answers which. If all core blocks are present, continue with: additional company mini-profiles, extra scenarios (base, upside, stress), and explicit assumption tables until the run ends, without repeating the same SWOT in different words.

SECTION 4 - CUSTOMER AND OFFERING STRUCTURE: Describe buyer types (enterprise, mid-market, public sector, consumer), purchase cycles, RFP behavior, and concentration of buying power. Cover packaging (bundles, platform fees, usage-based) and what moves willingness-to-pay in {year}.

SECTION 5 - ECONOMICS OF SUPPLY: Map fixed vs variable cost structure for typical vendors, scale economies, and where marginal cost curves flatten. Add capacity constraints (silicon, talent, data, energy) that could cap growth.

SECTION 6 - ECOSYSTEM AND STANDARDS: List consortia, file formats, APIs, and interoperability pressure. Note where regulation or procurement standards become design constraints for new entrants.

OVERFLOW: Company mini-profiles for tier-2 list (3-5 firms), a competitive feature matrix in prose, a "myths vs reality" list for the industry, and a stress case where two negative shocks (e.g. rate spike plus export control) hit simultaneously. Keep distinct content in each block.

GTM AND PACKAGING: Add a section comparing land-and-expand vs enterprise RFP, PLG, channel-led, and field-led GTM in this space in {year}, and which is winning for which segment.

UNIT ECONOMICS FOCUS: If applicable, add verbal ranges or proxies for CAC payback, gross margin at scale, and operating leverage, always with uncertainty labels.

IP AND OPEN SOURCE: Add IP risk: patent thickets, standards-essential claims, and open-source license contagion (copyleft) where the topic touches software or silicon; note defensive vs offensive patent posture of top players.

SUSTAINABILITY PRESSURE: Add how carbon disclosure, scope 1-3, or product lifecycle rules change buyer behavior or opex, even qualitatively.

COUNTER-POSITIONING: Add one subsection on insurgent business models that incumbents structurally under-price or cannot copy without cannibalization.

DILIGENCE Q LIST: Add 15-20 board-style diligence questions an acquirer would ask about the industry in {year}, each one line, grouped (market, product, GTM, legal, finance).
{output_guide}
tasks.expected_output: A deeper maximal analysis: all prior sections plus GTM and packaging, unit-economics proxies, IP and open source, sustainability pressure, counter-positioning, diligence question bank, and overflow profiles and stress tests, for the same topic, year, and planning scope.

tasks.description:
MISSION: You are the Trend Scout. Build a regionally decomposed, forward-looking view of "{topic}" in {year} that the synthesis can slice by geography without losing nuance. Open with a one-paragraph global thesis, then drill down. Do not collapse regions into a single adjective per continent.

NORTH AMERICA: Key demand drivers, regulatory or subsidy shifts, major customer or vendor behavior, and one under-reported local dynamic. Cite category-specific signals, not just macro.

ASIA-PACIFIC: Split when needed (e.g. China vs India vs rest). Growth patterns, supply chain and manufacturing angles, and digital adoption. Note cross-border data or cloud constraints if the topic is tech-heavy.

EUROPE: Regulatory and ESG or privacy overlays, single-market vs country variance, and energy or industrial policy if relevant. Flag Brexit or EU policy threads only when they change economics.

EMERGING MARKETS: At least one cluster of countries with outsized opportunity or risk; include adoption barriers (FX, skills, infrastructure).

CROSS-REGION: Compare demand, capex, investment pace, and adoption curves. State where the same vendor strategy wins vs must localize. Identify arbitrage: where margin pools sit vs where growth sits.

SIGNALS: Important surprises, accelerators, and constraints. A 12-month watchlist: at least 12 specific signals, each with why it matters and what would falsify a bullish or bearish read.

DEPTH RULE: For every region, include at least one mini-example (company, program, or policy) so the section does not read as abstract. Keep adding region-specific detail and cross-links until the token limit stops generation; avoid generic wrap-ups.

SUB-NATIONAL: Where it matters, add at least one metro, state, or free-trade zone angle (e.g. leading tech hub vs policy laggard) for North America and APAC to avoid over-smoothing.

TALENT AND MIGRATION: For each major region, add one bullet on skills shortage or brain gain/loss, visa or remote-work policy, and what that implies for {topic} in {year}.

CLIMATE, ENERGY, AND PHYSICAL FOOTPRINT: If the topic touches data centers, manufacturing, logistics, or materials, add regional power prices, water stress, or carbon policy hooks where they change site selection or opex.

INFRA AND CONNECTIVITY: Note broadband or 5G or trade-port constraints when they gate adoption, per region, even briefly.

HORIZON LAYERS: For each region, add a 12-24 month "near" vs 24-60 month "structural" view so synthesis can sequence investments.

TENSION MAP: Add a short section listing three-to-five cross-border tensions (e.g. data sovereignty vs open cloud, friend-shoring vs cost) that create winners and losers, with who benefits on each side.

EXTENDED WATCHLIST: Add six more potential signals (for 18 total) focused on second-order: supplier behavior, two-sided platforms, and financing conditions.

MIDDLE EAST, AFRICA, AND LATIN AMERICA: Add at least one dedicated subsection (combine if thin) for growth corridors, import substitution, policy, or energy-linked demand that affects the topic, with the same example discipline as other regions. If a region is immaterial, say so in one firm sentence and why.

FUNDING AND EXIT ENVIRONMENT: For venture-heavy or PE-heavy subsectors, add regional split of funding pace (public vs private, early vs late) and one line on what an IPO or SPAC window would mean in each region, without inventing deal lists.

CURRENCY: Note where FX translation materially flatters or depress growth, and which local pair matters most (e.g. JPY, CNY, MXN) for the topic in {year}.

COMPETITION POLICY: Add region-specific antitrust, subsidy, or industrial-policy moves that could reshape share in the next 24 months, with a concrete enforcement or filing example if known generically from public record patterns.

DEMOGRAPHICS: If consumer or labor demographics move demand (aging, youth bulge, urbanization), add a short cross-regional read.

SIGNAL DE-DUP: In a short closing subsection, name three pairs of watchlist signals that could be redundant and how you would not double-count them in synthesis.
{output_guide}
tasks.expected_output: A broader maximal regional report: prior regional depth plus MEA/LatAm coverage (or explicit immateriality), funding environment, currency effects, competition policy, demographics, 24+ watchlist items with de-dup notes, and full cross-links for the same topic and year.

tasks.description:
BRIEF: You are the Risk Assessor. Produce a detailed, board-ready risk map for "{topic}" in {year}. The matrix must be legible, comparable across categories, and tied to the economics of the industry, not just headlines.

REGULATORY (TOP 3+): At minimum cover EU, US, and China-anchored or comparable regulatory vectors relevant to the topic (substitute with accurate regional set if the industry is different). For each: nature of change, who is in scope, calendar or phase risk, and whether compliance is a fixed cost, variable cost, or strategic pivot. For each, add root cause, trigger events, early warning indicators, second-order supply-chain or go-to-market effects, responsible function, and mitigation with urgency (immediate vs 12-month horizon).

TECHNICAL (TOP 3+): e.g. model reliability, security, alignment, data leakage, long-tail failure modes, energy or cooling limits, or sector-specific science risk. For each, link to product, liability, and brand exposure. Use impact and probability in High/Medium/Low with a one-sentence calibration of what would move a rating up one notch.

GEOPOLITICAL (TOP 3+): e.g. semiconductors, export control, data localization, talent mobility, or conflict-driven demand swings. For each, map exposure by firm archetype, not just nation-state story.

CROSS-MATERIAL RISKS: If two risks compound (e.g. regulation + supply chain), add an explicit compounding section with scenario stress.

SURVEILLANCE: Ongoing monitoring table: what to track weekly vs quarterly. Include false-positive discipline so teams do not chase noise.

RANKING: Final prioritized stack rank with a narrative why the top three dominate capital allocation. Keep elaborating on triggers, owners, and mitigations until the model stops, without shrinking to a one-paragraph summary.

MARKET AND COUNTERPARTY: Add 2-3 risks for customer concentration, single-supplier, or platform dependency (app-store, cloud, or payments) with financial translation (DSO, take-rate exposure).

REPUTATION AND LITIGATION: If relevant, add product recall class, class-action, or ESG greenwash exposure with trigger examples from analog industries.

INSURANCE AND BALANCE-SHEET: Note insurability, deductibles, or covenant risks for levered players in a downturn, even qualitatively.

HUMAN AND ORG: Add People risks: key-person, strike, or unionization where material to {topic} in {year}.

ESCALATION LADDER: Define five severity levels with example events for the top risk category, so product and GTM can align on response playbooks in prose.

RISK BUDGET: Suggest a notional time or capex budget teams should set aside to mitigate top-tier risks, expressed as ranges or "order-of-magnitude" categories if numbers are unknown.

CYBER, DATA, AND RESILIENCE: Add explicit cyber and data-breach or ransomware exposure for the industry supply chain, third-party SaaS, and on-prem footprint; connect to business continuity, ransomware insurance, and mean-time-to-restore in qualitative terms for {year}.

PHYSICAL AND OPERATIONAL: If manufacturing, plants, or logistics are central, add natural disaster, pandemic-style labor absenteeism, and port or rail disruption as a tagged cluster with H/M/L on revenue impact, even if only directional.

WARRANTY, LIABILITY, AND RECALL: Where physical products or safety matter, add recall, warranty reserve, and strict-liability style risks with a generic analog; avoid naming ongoing litigation you cannot verify.

AUDIT, ACCOUNTING, AND RESTATEMENT: For sectors with long contracts or aggressive revenue recognition, add risk of restatement, channel stuffing, or audit qualification as a low-probability, high-scenario narrative.

TAIL RISK PRESENTATION: Add a one-paragraph description of a true tail event (multi-sigma) that would invalidate the base case, without predicting probability numerically, and which existing mitigations are useless against it (so the board can see the gap).

RISK-TO-OKR MAPPING: For the top 5 risks, add one line each mapping to a hypothetical company OKR or metric that would go red if the risk materialized.
{output_guide}
tasks.expected_output: A full-spectrum risk package: all prior rows plus cyber, physical or BC, warranty and liability, audit and revenue-quality tails, tail narrative, risk-to-OKR mapping, escalation ladder, stack rank, budget, and surveillance, with 16+ row-level entries where applicable, for the same topic and year.

tasks.description:
CONSOLIDATION: You are the Report Synthesizer. You have four upstream streams for the same topic / year: (1) Data sheet - market statistics, segments, and region splits; (2) Deep analysis - technology, competition, and strategic recommendations; (3) Regional trends - per-region and cross-region; (4) Risk assessment - matrix and monitoring. The topic context is "{topic}" in {year}. Do not re-run research; preserve every non-redundant number, name, and nuance. If two streams disagree, do not pick arbitrarily: explain the conflict, the likely resolution path, and what additional data would settle it. If a stream is thin, say so and avoid invented precision.

REQUIRED SKELETON: Executive summary (aim ~250-320 words) that names the top five takeaways, the top three risks, and the top three opportunities. Market overview: integrate TAM, CAGR, segments, and top players from the data stream with the strategic framing from deep analysis, without double-counting. Technology and competitive landscape: condense the deep analysis into an exec-readable narrative, keeping SWOT and moat logic. Regional trends: digest the Trend Scout into a skimmable geographic section with 2-3 bullets per major region. Risk assessment: import the risk matrix, then add a synthesis-level "so what" for a CFO and a tech executive. Strategic recommendations: merge ranked themes from deep analysis with data-backed sizing and risk-adjusted phasing; add an implementation phasing view (0-12 vs 12-36 months). Sources: unified bibliography style, de-duplicated, with a note on which claims rest on weaker evidence.

QUALITY BAR: The report must read as one voice. Define acronyms once. Normalize units (USD, years, %). Call out any figure that is a forecast vs actual. The document must be suitable for a board or executive staff meeting without an appendix, though you may use footnote-style asides in-line.

COMPLETENESS: Ensure no data stream is orphaned: every major bullet from the data dossier, every major technology vector from the deep analysis, every region block from the trend scan, and every risk group from the risk workstream must be reflected, merged, or explicitly deferred with reason.

READER VIEWS: Add a 10-line "CFO take" and a 10-line "CTO take" after the executive summary, each in bullets, with zero new facts (only re-emphasis and framing).

ANALYTICS INTEGRITY: Add a one-page equivalent subsection "Provenance and conflicts" that lists 5-8 specific merged claims with which upstream block they came from, and one merged conflict you resolved (or could not) with a clear statement of residual uncertainty.

OPTIONAL ANNEX-STYLE: If space allows, add "Figures to build next week" (a short list of charts that would make the report stronger) without inventing numbers, and a "further work" list scoped to 90 days, aligned to the four streams only.

TONE AND LEGAL: Avoid forward-looking language that pretends to be a securities filing; add one sentence disclaimer-style boundary that the synthesis is research consolidation, not investment advice, without sounding like boilerplate from every paragraph.

BOARD Q&A: Add a section "Expected board Q&A" with 12-15 tough questions a skeptical board member would ask, each followed by a 2-3 sentence answer using only material already merged from the four streams; if an answer is unknown, say so plainly.

INFORMATION GAPS: Add "What we still do not know" with at least 8 specific gaps, each tagged with which workstream would have closed it, and a rough effort estimate (S/M/L) to close in the real world.

M&A OR STRATEGY LENS: Add a 12-line section "Implications for a consolidator or new entrant" that references only the merged facts; do not name fictional transactions.

ER/IR ANGLE: Add a 10-line subsection on how a public company in this space would frame the themes on an earnings call (risks, opportunities, and metrics to emphasize), without fabricating company-specific forward guidance numbers.

ENTRANT WATCH: Name 3-5 archetypal disrupter profiles (e.g. vertical SaaS, hyperscaler, open core, national champion) and which merged facts support that profile becoming material in 18-36 months, without inventing new firms.

TERMINOLOGY CONSISTENCY: Add a 6-item micro-glossary in-line for terms that the four streams may have used with different words, harmonized for the final reader.
{output_guide}
{long_output_guide}
tasks.expected_output: A fully expanded long-form report: all prior sections plus board Q&A, explicit information gaps, consolidator/entrant lens, earnings-call framing, disrupter archetypes with evidence-only support, term harmonization, provenance, CFO/CTO views, and disclaimer; single voice, same topic and year, no new unsourced research claims.
